subModules.title: Reading Mission: Mastering Nuanced Reporting Verbs
subModules.grammarFocus: Advanced Reported Speech with Specific Verbs

content.summary: Welcome to your reading mission on advanced reported speech. In this lesson, you will read an engaging story about a school newspaper investigation. You will learn how to move beyond basic reporting with 'say' and 'tell' by discovering precise reporting verbs that show admission, warning, refusal, and apology.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Verb patterns including to-infinitive, object plus to-infinitive, and gerunds after reporting verbs.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Nuanced verbs used for reporting statements, questions, and commands in everyday contexts.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning text for specific verb structures and understanding character motivations in dialogue-heavy narratives.

learningObjectives: Understand the main events in a short B1 narrative about a school newspaper investigation.
Locate specific reporting verbs and their grammatical patterns in context.
Recognize how verbs like admit, warn, and refuse change the meaning of reported statements.

contextWarmup.prompt: When someone shares a secret with you at school, what is the best way to handle it?
options: Keep it strictly confidential and never share it with anyone.
Tell your closest friends immediately during lunch break.
Post about it on social media to see what people think.
contextWarmup.explanation: Keeping a secret confidential shows trustworthiness and builds strong friendships, which is the correct choice in personal communication.

rules: Verb + to-infinitive: Used with verbs such as offer, promise, refuse, and agree. Example: He offered to help me.
Verb + object + to-infinitive: Used with verbs such as warn, advise, remind, and invite. Example: She advised me to study harder.
Verb + -ing or preposition + -ing: Used with verbs such as admit, deny, and apologize for. Example: He admitted making a mistake.

commonTrap.explanation: Students often try to use 'that' clauses with every reporting verb, similar to basic 'say' or 'tell'. However, many precise reporting verbs require specific infinitive or gerund structures.
commonTrap.wrong: He refused that he would go to the meeting.
commonTrap.correct: He refused to go to the meeting.

paragraphs: Last Monday, a strange thing happened at Oakridge High School. The monthly student newspaper disappeared from the printer room before anyone could read it. Leo, the chief editor, was extremely worried. He gathered his team and began investigating who took the copies. At first, nobody wanted to speak about the incident.

Later that afternoon, Mark admitted taking the papers because he disagreed with the main article. The head teacher advised Mark to apologize for his actions immediately. Mark apologized for causing trouble and promised to help print new copies the next morning. Leo accepted his apology and warned everyone to talk openly if they had future disagreements.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Nuanced Reporting Verbs in Action

content.summary: Focus on how speakers use precise reporting verbs like admit, refuse, warn, and promise instead of basic words like say or tell. Pay attention to the specific patterns that follow these verbs, such as gerunds or infinitives, when listening to fast conversational English.
learningObjectives: Catch the main topic of a spoken conversation about workplace meetings and commitments.
Identify specific reporting verbs used to convey admissions, refusals, warnings, and promises.
Notice how words link together in fast connected speech involving reporting structures.

keyPhrases.note: Followed by a gerund when reporting a past action.
Followed by an infinitive with 'to' for direct rejections.
Used with an object pronoun and a negative infinitive.
Used to express willingness to help or perform an action.

connectedSpeech.note: The final /d/ sound in admitted connects smoothly with the following /m/ sound.
The final /d/ in warned links directly to the vowel sound in us.
The preposition to is reduced to a weak schwa sound.
The infinitive marker to loses its full vowel value in natural speech.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Advanced Reported Speech with Nuanced Reporting Verbs

content.summary: Mastering precise reporting verbs in English allows you to convey intent, warnings, apologies, and promises without relying on basic 'say' or 'tell' structures. This guide covers the three major grammatical patterns for reporting verbs at the B1 level.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Verb + to-infinitive
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + Reporting Verb (offer, promise, refuse, threaten, agree) + to-infinitive
blueprintItems.example: He offered to carry my heavy suitcase upstairs.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Verb + object + to-infinitive
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + Reporting Verb (warn, advise, remind, encourage, persuade, invite) + Object + to-infinitive
blueprintItems.example: She advised me to study the grammar rules before the test.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Verb + -ing / preposition + -ing
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + Reporting Verb (admit, deny, suggest) or Verb + Preposition (apologize for, insist on, accuse of) + -ing form
blueprintItems.example: He apologized for arriving late to the important meeting.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always include the correct preposition after reporting verbs that require one before the -ing form.
mechanicsRules.badExample: She apologized being late to the interview.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: She apologized for being late to the interview.
mechanicsRules.why: Verbs like 'apologize' take the preposition 'for' before an -ing clause in English.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place the object directly between the reporting verb and the to-infinitive in pattern two.
mechanicsRules.badExample: He advised to start the project early.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: He advised his team to start the project early.
mechanicsRules.why: Verbs such as 'advise', 'remind', and 'warn' need a direct object before the infinitive verb.

mechanicsRules.rule: Keep the negative particle 'not' before the to-infinitive when reporting negative instructions.
mechanicsRules.badExample: She warned us to not touch the hot stove.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: She warned us not to touch the hot stove.
mechanicsRules.why: In formal and standard English grammar, 'not' comes directly before 'to' in infinitive clauses.

David promised to help me clean the garage tomorrow.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using the reporting verb 'advise' with an object and to-infinitive:
practicumQuestions.promptText: "You should study for the exam early," the teacher told Anna.
targetAnswers: The teacher advised Anna to study for the exam early.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The verb 'advise' requires an object (Anna) before the to-infinitive clause (to study).

Mark apologized for breaking your favorite coffee mug.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Apologize is followed by the preposition 'for' and then the gerund (-ing) form of the verb.

practicumQuestions.promptText: She refused working on the weekend without extra pay.

targetAnswers: Kevin admitted taking the last slice of cake from the fridge.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Admit is followed directly by the gerund (-ing) form of the action.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Choose the correct reporting verb pattern to complete the sentence: 'The travel agent encouraged us ...'
practicumQuestions.promptText: Complete the sentence with a correct object and infinitive: The travel agent encouraged us _____ early.
practicumQuestions.hint: Encourage takes an object and a to-infinitive.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Encourage follows the pattern: Subject + verb + object + to-infinitive.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the preposition error in the following sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Tom insisted in paying for our dinner last night.
practicumQuestions.hint: Insist takes a different preposition before an -ing clause.
targetAnswers: Tom insisted on paying for our dinner last night.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The correct collocation in English is 'insist on' followed by the -ing form.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Report the following direct speech using 'warn' with an object and negative infinitive:
practicumQuestions.promptText: "Don't swim in the deep end of the pool," the lifeguard said to the children.
targetAnswers: The lifeguard warned the children not to swim in the deep end of the pool.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Negative warnings with 'warn' take an object followed by 'not to' and the base verb.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the direct speech using the reporting verb 'offer' with a to-infinitive:
practicumQuestions.promptText: "Shall I carry these heavy bags for you?" Paul asked.
targetAnswers: Paul offered to carry those heavy bags for me.
Paul offered to carry these heavy bags for me.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Offers are reported using 'offer' followed directly by the to-infinitive ('to carry').

content.summary: Mastering nuanced reporting verbs requires precise word stress and clear articulation. Instead of relying on basic verbs like say or tell, precise verbs such as admit, warn, and refuse carry specific syllables that demand clear voice projection. Pay attention to how sentence stress shifts when you report statements, commands, or apologies to sound natural and confident.
content.audioGuidance: Focus on pausing slightly after reporting verbs to let the listener absorb the action. Ensure that unstressed syllables in multisyllabic reporting verbs like apologize are reduced correctly, while stressed syllables carry higher pitch and louder volume.

pillars.name: Syllable Stress in Reporting Verbs
pillars.target: Correct stress placement on multi-syllable reporting verbs
pillars.explanation: Verbs like ad-MIT, re-MIND, and a-POL-o-gize have specific stress patterns. Placing stress on the wrong syllable makes your spoken reported speech difficult for listeners to understand.

pillars.name: Reporting Intonation
pillars.target: Falling intonation for statements, rising intonation for warnings
pillars.explanation: When you report what someone said, your voice should drop at the end of neutral statements like admissions or denials. When you report warnings or strong advice, keep your voice firm and engaged.

pillars.name: Linking and Chunking
pillars.target: Smooth transition from reporting verb to the following infinitive or gerund
pillars.explanation: Link the final consonant of the reporting verb to the vowel sound of the next word, such as in the phrase warned us or apologized for, to maintain conversational flow.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice that the main stress remains on the second syllable when adding past tense suffixes.
The primary stress shifts to the fourth syllable in the continuous form.
The stress moves to the first syllable when the word functions as a noun instead of a verb.
The stress stays on the second syllable when shifting from verb to noun form.
